newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Dec 2.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Dec 2.

text.p: The delay in getting a government after the election has helped rob New Zealanders of their enthusiasm for the MMP (Mixed Member Proportional) voting system, according to UMR Insight polling results issued on Monday. The poll shows more New Zealanders now prefer the first-past-the-post system of electing Parliament than the mixed-member-proportional system used, for the first time, this year. UMR Insight joint managing director Stephen Mills said the latest result could be attributed to restlessness about the coalition talks "to some degree". Page 1.

NZ First was in a "no-win situation" because whichever way it went in a coalition, it would disappoint a significant number of people, NZ First leader Winston Peters told a rally in Tauranga on Sunday. He said NZ First would announce its decision "in a few days -- or a few weeks". "It's an awesome responsibility, and we're here to report today that we're almost there," Peters said. He defended his refusal to rush the talks, saying the outcome had to be a "durable" relationship. Page 1

Confidence is weakening within National and Labour that NZ First will be able to choose a coalition partner before parliament sits next week. Though parliament is due to meet by December 13 at the latest, sources in both main parties are increasingly reluctant to predict that a coalition will be formed before then. Labour leader Helen Clark has even floated the idea that parliament could appoint an interim Speaker and adjourn, allowing the coalition process to continue over the Christmas break. Page 2.
NZ First's former parliamentary aide Terry Heffernan has lashed out at personal criticism of him by former colleague Michael Laws over why he is no longer working for the party. Page 2.

Retailer Progressive Enterprises expects to restore payment of an interim dividend. Chairman Don Humphreys told shareholders at the annual meeting in Auckland that group after-tax profit for the first quarter was well ahead of the same period last year. Progressive suspended interim dividend payments last year after a 79 percent plunge in bottom-line earnings in the six months to January 28. Page 20.

Liquor sales remained soft, but Lion Nathan's new beer Leopard Black had not affected DB Group's sales, managing director Erik Korthals Altes said. "October was slightly ahead. November doesn't look that good on last year. The two look about flat on last year." he said. "December, however, is still an open book." In November, Korthals Altes said total beer consumption in the year to September had been down 2.1 percent on the year before, largely due to an atrocious winter. Page 20.
Investment company Strathmore Group has increased its stake in CES Communications to 36 percent, from 20 percent, through the exercise of an option. Page 20.

Wholesale sales increased two percent to $12.08 billion in the September quarter, compared with $11.85 billion for the same period in 1995, Statistics New Zealand said. "This was the eighth consecutive quarter to record an increase when compared with the same time in the previous year," it said. Page 21.

NZ First on Sunday began a damage-control programme in advance of its coalition decision, which is being delayed by mountains of policy paperwork. Some in Labour are interpreting the damage control as laying the groundwork for a coalition with National, believing that choosing National is the only option that would necessitate it. In Tauranga, NZ First leader Winston Peters told 400 supporters and nine of his 17 MPs that his party was in a no-win situation. "We are going to disappoint a great number of our supporters...It doesn't matter what we do; that's inevitable," Peters said.

The biggest obstacle to a Labour-NZ First coalition deal -- NZ First's unease at Labour's spending intentions -- is likely to grow a little bigger on Monday when the Treasury publishes its latest forecasts. The December Economic and Fiscal Update will track events since the pre-election opening of the books on September 12. The caretaker Finance Minister Bill Birch said the outlook would remain "positive and robust" and that any differences between the two sets of numbers would be slight. But although the changes will be small, they are all headed in the wrong direction with Birch having signalled the projected
surpluses for this and subsequent years will be revised down.

The Alliance executive council on Sunday gave the caucus the go-ahead to discuss with Labour terms for supporting a Labour-NZ First coalition government. Alliance leader Jim Anderton said the decision had been endorsed unanimously.

The New Zealand banking system may be heading for another major shakeout as the parents of key players prepare for an overhaul of the Australian financial sector. Among the likely recommendations of the Wallis banking inquiry in March, is a
relaxation of Australia's present laws preventing mergers of the nation's four biggest banks and two largest insurers, most of which have substantial New Zealand holdings.

A communications system developed by Christchurch-based CES Communications, 36 percent owned by Strathmore Group, is to be tested by the United States National Aeronautics and Space Administration. This is a major opportunity for CES to prove its technology internationally, Strathmore chairman Ray Thomson said.

Intense competition among pharmaceutical wholesalers resulted in Zuellig New Zealand reporting a four percent larger loss of $946,000 in the September six months. Chairman Brian Allison has said there were too many warehouses supplying the pharmaceutical industry, and the sector's cost structure was too high and needed rationalisation.
